title: I'm scared about the future
seoTitle: Scared About the Future? What the Bible Says About Fear
description: Afraid of what's coming? What Isaiah 41:10, Psalm 23, and Psalm 91 really promise about fear, and small steps to take this week when the future feels dark.
summary: For the dread that won't let go of tomorrow: what Scripture promises about the future, what it doesn't, and what to do this week.
askedAs: What does the Bible say about fear?
answer: You're scared of what's coming, and you can't talk yourself out of it. Maybe the fear has a name: the money, a diagnosis, your kids, the country. Maybe it's everywhere at once, a dread that moves from one worry to the next and gets loudest at night. You're not foolish for feeling it, and you're not faithless. Some of what you fear is real. But fear tells the future as if the worst were already settled and as if you'll face it alone, and neither is true. Tonight, don't try to solve the whole future. Write down the one thing you're most afraid of, ask whether there's one thing you can do about it this week, and hand the rest to God in plain words. He said “Do not fear, for I am with you” (Isaiah 41:10) to people in exile, not to people who were safe.
happening:
Fear of the future rarely stays in one place. It might start with something specific, a scan you're waiting on, a rumor of layoffs, a child who's struggling, and then spread to the economy, the country, the world your kids will inherit. It gets loud in the quiet moments, in the car or at two in the morning when the phone is finally down. Your mind runs the scenarios, always the bad ones, until each feels less like a possibility than a preview. Your body joins in with a tight chest, a knot in your stomach, and sleep that won't come or won't stay.

The usual explanations each get something right. Doctors will tell you the body carries an alarm built to keep you alive, and it can fire at a danger twenty years away as if it were in the room. Counselors will tell you the mind fills an unknown future with the worst it can imagine, and that uncertainty itself can be harder to bear than bad news. If the fear has become constant, or it comes as panic, that side of it deserves a doctor's attention, and the page on [anxiety and worry that won't switch off](/help/anxiety) goes further.

The church often adds a spiritual explanation: fear means weak faith, and the cure is to trust God more. There's truth in that too. Scripture tells God's people over and over not to be afraid, and fear can show you where you've put your trust. But that explanation forgets who first heard the command. It was spoken to people facing armies, exile, and death, and it usually came with a reason, as when God told Isaac, “Do not be afraid, for I am with you” (Genesis 26:24). Jesus himself was “sorrowful and deeply distressed” the night before he died (Matthew 26:37). So the feeling itself can't be the sin, though what the fear is allowed to do may become one.

What all three explanations leave out is that fear of the future is often love looking ahead. You're afraid because there are people and things in that future you care about, and you can't protect them from here. I'm raising five sons, so I won't write about the world they'll inherit as if it were someone else's problem. The question under the fear isn't only whether the bad thing will happen. It's whether anyone will be there when it does, and whether the future belongs to anyone at all.

scripture.intro: The verses people reach for when they're afraid are some of the best known in the Bible, and some of the most often lifted out of where they sit. Read in their setting, they grow stronger. They were spoken to people in real trouble, and they promise God's company where you're afraid to go.

passages.text: Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you; I will surely help you; I will uphold you with My right hand of righteousness.
passages.reading: This part of Isaiah is addressed to God's people in exile in Babylon. They had lost their land, their temple, and their king, and they had begun to say, “My way is hidden from the LORD” (Isaiah 40:27). God begins with who they are before he says a word about what will happen: “I have chosen and not rejected you” (Isaiah 41:9). Then come the promises: presence, strength, help, and a hand that holds them up. There's no date and no forecast. The command not to fear rests on God's presence, “for I am with you,” and it was spoken to people for whom the worst had already happened.

passages.text: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.
passages.reading: The psalm carries David's name, and David was a shepherd before he was a king. The “paths of righteousness” of verse 3 lead straight into the valley of verse 4, and through it. The Hebrew word behind “shadow of death” can also mean deep darkness, and Scripture uses it for distress and extreme danger as well as for death, so the valley is death and everything that feels like it. Notice the grammar. For three verses the singer talks about God: “He leads me,” “He restores my soul.” In the valley he starts talking to him: “for You are with me.” The dark is where theology turns into prayer. The rod drove off predators and the staff guided the sheep. The valley was no shorter for it, but the shepherd stayed close enough to feel.

passages.text: He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty. I will say to the LORD, “You are my refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust.”
passages.reading: Psalm 91 was written to be prayed, and the Gospels show how to hold its sweeping promises. On the pinnacle of the temple, the devil quoted this psalm's promise of angels and dared Jesus to jump (Matthew 4:5-6). Jesus answered, “Do not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7), words from Deuteronomy that recall Israel at Massah demanding, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (Exodus 17:7). Fear wants a rescue as proof that God is near. Jesus refused to demand one, then went to the cross, where God brought him through death. The psalm itself says, “I will be with him in trouble” (Psalm 91:15). The people who live in its shelter still meet trouble. They never meet it alone.

passages.text: I heard and trembled within; my lips quivered at the sound. Decay entered my bones; I trembled where I stood. Yet I must wait patiently for the day of distress to come upon the people who invade us. Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though the sheep are cut off from the fold and no cattle are in the stalls, yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!
passages.reading: Habakkuk complained to God about violence and injustice, and God's answer was worse than the complaint: Babylon was coming (Habakkuk 1:6). So the prophet knew the future, and it was terrible, and you can see what that knowledge did to his body: his lips quivered, decay entered his bones, and he trembled where he stood. Then he named everything that could fail, fig and vine, olive and field, flock and herd, which in his world was the grocery store and the retirement account at once. He couldn't rejoice in the outcome, because he knew what it would be, so he rejoiced in God. That's the difference between optimism and hope: optimism bets on the fig tree, and hope holds on to God when the fig tree fails. Habakkuk trembled, and then he said yet.

passages.text: Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Today has enough trouble of its own.
passages.reading: Jesus says this at the end of a passage in the Sermon on the Mount about birds, flowers, food, and clothes, all resting on one line: “your heavenly Father knows that you need them” (Matthew 6:32). Notice how realistic he is: tomorrow will have its own trouble. A few verses earlier he taught his disciples to ask for bread one day at a time (Matthew 6:11), the way Israel gathered manna, enough for each day (Exodus 16:4). Worry drags tomorrow's trouble into today, where you can't do anything with it, and it comes without the grace God gives on the day itself.

passages.text: Now since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death.
passages.reading: Under most fear of the future lies the last future, the one none of us will miss, and Hebrews calls the fear of it a lifelong slavery. The letter was written to Christians who had already lost property and stood by friends in prison (Hebrews 10:32-34), so it knows what danger is. Its answer is that the Son of God took on flesh and blood, went into death himself, and broke the power of the one who holds death over us. The fear loosens when you know someone has gone through death ahead of you and come out the other side. That's why Christian hope rests on an event you can examine, an empty tomb on a Sunday morning, rather than a mood you have to keep up.

whyHard:
People have always been afraid of the future, and they've usually had good reason. Several of the passages above were first heard by people with more cause for dread than most of us have: exiles, a prophet awaiting an invasion, Christians who had lost their property for their faith. What has changed is what we have to carry the fear with.

For centuries in the West, ordinary people lived inside a story about where time was going. The Christian story ran from creation to new creation and ended with judgment, resurrection, and a world set right. In the modern era a second story grew up beside it and, for many, replaced it: history as progress, each generation better off than the last, with science and prosperity steadily repairing what was broken. You didn't need God to feel good about the future; the trend lines were enough. Many of us in the church lived on that second story more than we'd admit, and that story has been wearing thin. When people stop believing the future is going somewhere, it stops being a story and becomes a forecast, and no one can live inside a forecast.

I came to faith from atheism, and I won't pretend unbelievers have no way to face the future. Some face it with real courage, looking straight at a universe they believe is indifferent and choosing to live well anyway. That courage deserves respect. What it can't offer is company beyond ourselves, and underneath most fear of the future is the fear of facing it alone.

Then there's what we let into our heads. For almost all of history, news of a faraway disaster arrived late or never. Now a disaster anywhere on earth can reach your pocket within minutes, delivered by apps designed to keep you looking, and fear keeps people looking better than almost anything. We end up feeling responsible for everything while able to change almost nothing, and dread is what that feels like from the inside. We call it staying informed, though much of it is rehearsal.

It's harder still when no one seems to be steering. The future felt steadier when people trusted someone at the wheel: government, the markets, the press, the church. Much of that trust has eroded, and some of it was lost for good reason, because institutions, churches among them, betrayed the people who trusted them. We don't get to stand outside that indictment. Christians have lived through a shaking like this before. When the Visigoths sacked Rome in 410, people who had assumed the city would stand forever were stunned, and some blamed the Christians. Augustine answered with *The City of God*, arguing that the cities and empires of this world rise and fall, and that the city of God, made up of all who love God, is one no army can sack. Rather than reassuring his readers about Rome, he told them where to put their weight.

The last layer belongs to us. A great deal of American Christianity has offered faith as insurance: trust God and things will go well, claim the promise and the bad thing won't come. We printed Jeremiah 29:11 on graduation cards and forgot it was first sent to exiles told to build houses in Babylon, because Babylon's seventy years had to run their course before God would bring his people home (Jeremiah 29:5, 10). We prayed Psalm 91 as though it were a charm. Pastors, and I include myself, are tempted to preach that version because frightened people want to hear it. But a faith that promised safety has nothing to say when the future turns dark, or it says the cruelest thing possible: *you didn't believe enough*. Scripture made a different promise. Facing the furnace, three young men told the king of Babylon their God could save them, “But even if He does not,” they would not bow (Daniel 3:17-18). They went into the fire, and a fourth figure walked with them there (Daniel 3:25).

The future was never safe. It has always been held.

thisWeek.intro: You can't settle the future this week, and you don't have to. These small, faithful steps put it back where it belongs, in God's hands and one day at a time. Start the first tonight; it takes five minutes and a pen.

steps.title: Write the fear down in one sentence
steps.body: Fear likes to stay vague, because a fog can't be answered. Finish the sentence *I'm afraid that...* on paper, as specifically as you can, and list every fear if there are several. Naming a fear shrinks it to a size you can pray about. If yours has a specific name, Find Help has a place to start for [a hard diagnosis](/help?need=diagnosis), [a lost job](/help?need=job-loss), and [money trouble](/help?need=money).

steps.title: Sort what's yours from what isn't
steps.body: Ask of each fear: is there one thing I can do about this in the next seven days? If there is, write it down and do it: make the appointment, call about the bill, update the will, have the conversation you've been avoiding. That's prudence, and Scripture honors it: “The prudent see danger and take cover” (Proverbs 22:3). If there's nothing to do this week, the fear isn't yours to carry this week. Circle it.

steps.title: Pray the circled fears, then tell someone
steps.body: Tell God the circled fears in plain words, then pray back to him the promise of Isaiah 41:10 or the confession of Psalm 23:4. If you have no words, pray Psalm 23 slowly as your own. You'll likely pick the fear back up tomorrow; put it down again, which is what casting your anxiety on him looks like (1 Peter 5:7). Then tell one person who loves you what you're afraid of, and ask them to pray for you by name.

steps.title: Put the news on a schedule
steps.body: Pick one time a day for the news, a source that informs more than it alarms, and a limit you'll keep. Turn off breaking-news alerts, and keep the news out of the first hour of your morning and the last hour before bed. You'll still know enough to pray for the world and love your neighbor, which is what the news is for. [How to Unhook From Your Screens](/how-tos/body-how-to-unhook-from-your-screens) can help.

steps.title: Do one thing that assumes a future
steps.body: To his people in Babylon, God said through Jeremiah, “Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce” (Jeremiah 29:5). Hope often starts in the hands before it reaches the heart. Do one small thing this week that assumes God will still be there tomorrow: plant something, make plans with a friend, write a letter for someone you love to open years from now. Fear says the future is closed. Small acts of hope answer it.

moreHelp.body:
Fear of the future is part of being human, and most of the time it belongs with prayer, friendship, and wiser habits. But if the dread is there most days for weeks, if it comes as panic, if it's costing you sleep, work, or the people you love, or if it has turned into hopelessness, it's time to see a doctor or a licensed counselor. That isn't a failure of faith. Your body and mind are part of what God made, and caring for them is part of trusting him.

Start with your family doctor, who can look for physical causes and refer you. Your insurance company keeps a directory of covered counselors, and a pastor who knows your area often knows which counselors are good. If you want one who shares your faith, ask, and ask whether they're licensed in your state; most state licensing boards let you check online. A licensed counselor who is also a Christian gives you both.
signs: The dread is there most days for weeks, even when things are going well.
Fear comes as panic: a pounding heart, trouble breathing, a sudden sense that something terrible is about to happen. If a doctor hasn't checked these symptoms, get care right away.
You can't sleep, eat, or work, or you're avoiding ordinary things like the mail or the doctor because of what you might find.
You're drinking or using something to quiet the fear.
The fear has turned into hopelessness or thoughts of ending your life. Call or text 988 now, or 911 if you're in danger.
What you fear is a legal or money deadline, like foreclosure or a lawsuit. Talk to a lawyer, a legal aid office, or a nonprofit credit counselor this week.

Someone has threatened you or your family. If you're in danger now, call 911. If it's someone at home, the National Domestic Violence Hotline (on Find Help) can help you plan for safety; otherwise, report it to the police.
moreHelp.firstCall: Plain words are enough: *I've been afraid about the future for a few months. It's affecting my sleep and my work, and I'd like to talk to someone.* Say how long it's been going on and what it's keeping you from. Then ask: *Are you licensed in this state? Do you take my insurance or offer a sliding scale? Have you worked with anxiety before?* If faith matters to you, ask whether they're comfortable with it being part of your conversations.
moreHelp.cost: Cost stops many people before they ask, so ask. Many insurance plans cover counseling; call the number on your card and ask about mental health benefits. If you're paying yourself, ask about sliding-scale fees. Community mental health centers and university training clinics, where supervised graduate students see clients, usually cost less. Your employer may offer an employee assistance program with a few free sessions, and many churches keep a benevolence fund for exactly this.

helping.body:
If someone you love is scared of the future, the first gift is to listen long enough to learn what the fear actually is; it's usually more specific than it sounds. Don't argue with the fear or hurry to fix it, and be careful with reassurance: *it'll be fine* is a promise you can't keep, and they know it. Offer what God offered the exiles, which was presence: *I don't know what's going to happen, and I'm not going anywhere.* Then help them find one thing to do this week, and do it alongside them.

If you're a parent, remember that children read the adults around them more closely than the headlines, and you don't have to pretend the world is safe. What steadies them is watching someone they love admit to being afraid and keep praying and planting anyway. If you're a pastor, many of your people are being taught to fear by their screens; read these texts with them in context and refuse to preach the safety version. [How Do You Pastor a Church Addicted to Cable News?](/writing/pastoring-a-captured-congregation) goes further.
say: What's the part you're most afraid of?
That's a real fear. You're not foolish for feeling it.
I can't promise it won't happen. I can promise I won't leave you alone in it.
Is there one thing we could do about it this week?
Can I pray with you, or would you rather I just sit with you?
dontSay: It'll all work out, I promise.
If you really trusted God, you wouldn't be afraid.
The Bible says not to be afraid, so stop.
Other people have it much worse.
helping.next: Check in again in a few days, at night if they'll let you, since that's when fear tends to return. Offer something practical rather than more words: a ride, a meal, company at the appointment. Pray for them by name and tell them you are. If you notice the signs listed under getting more help, say so kindly and offer to help them make the call. If they mention ending their life, stay with them and call or text 988 together, or call 911 if they're in immediate danger.

prayer:
Lord, I don't know what's coming, and I'm afraid of it. You know the list I carry better than I do: the money, the people I love, my own body, a world that seems to be coming apart. I've rehearsed the worst so often it feels like memory.

I won't pretend with you. You heard Habakkuk tremble and didn't send him away. Hear me.

You never promised me a safe tomorrow. You promised to be in it. So be in it. Be in the room when the news comes, whatever it is. Walk with me through the valley I'm afraid to enter, and hold the people I love when I can't reach them.

Give me bread for today, and teach me to trust you for tomorrow's bread tomorrow. What I can't carry, I give to you, and when I take it back tonight, help me give it to you again.

Your Son went through death ahead of me and came out the other side. You are already in the future I'm afraid of. Meet me there.

In Jesus' name, amen.

faq.q: Is it a sin to be afraid of the future?
faq.a: Feeling afraid isn't a sin. Hebrews says Jesus “offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death” (Hebrews 5:7), and he was without sin. Scripture does tell God's people not to be afraid, but it gives a reason: “for I am with you” (Isaiah 41:10). Fear becomes a spiritual problem when it takes the wheel, making your decisions, shrinking your love, or convincing you God has gone. Then the answer is honesty with him, the way the Psalms pray.

faq.q: What if the thing I'm afraid of actually happens?
faq.a: Then God will be in it with you, and it won't be the end of your story. The promises about fear in Scripture were spoken to people in exile, in the valley, facing prison, and on the night before the crucifixion (John 14:27). Grace tends to come on the day it's needed, the way manna did, which is one reason the future you imagine can feel unbearable: you're picturing tomorrow's trouble with today's strength. And for those who belong to Christ, even death has been walked through ahead of them (Hebrews 2:14-15).

faq.q: Will God protect me and my family?
faq.a: God's protection is real, and Scripture invites you to ask for it boldly; Psalm 91 gives you the words. But the Bible never promises that nothing bad will happen to people who trust him. Jesus told his disciples some of them would be put to death, and in the same breath said, “Yet not even a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:16-18). He meant a deeper keeping, the kind Paul describes when he says that nothing, “neither the present nor the future,” can separate us from the love of God (Romans 8:38-39). So pray for protection, and trust him with the answer.

faq.q: Is it wrong to plan for the future?
faq.a: No. Scripture commends preparation. Proverbs sends the slacker to learn from the ant, which stores food in summer (Proverbs 6:6-8), and Jesus takes it for granted that a builder sits down first to count the cost (Luke 14:28). Saving, insurance, a will, and a checkup are stewardship. The letter of James adds the humility that keeps planning honest: “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that” (James 4:15). The line runs between planning and worrying: planning makes a decision today and then rests, while worry keeps rehearsing a future it can't change. A simple test: does this thought lead to something you can do this week? If it does, do it. If it doesn't, it has stopped being planning, so hand it to God.

faq.q: Are we living in the end times?
faq.a: In one sense, yes: the New Testament calls the whole time since Christ came “these last days” (Hebrews 1:2). But no one can tell you when the end will come, and Jesus said so himself: “No one knows about that day or hour” (Matthew 24:36). The historic creeds, which the great Christian traditions share, confess that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead. Christians disagree, faithfully, about the timeline, and generation after generation has produced people certain the end had come. The end Scripture describes is a King's return and a world set right, and the New Testament writers described it to persecuted churches to give them hope. [How the Story Ends](/studyguides/end-times) sets out the main views fairly.

slots.note: James could add, in his own words, what fear for his five sons' future has looked like in his own home and what he does with it. The page stands without it.

James could add how he faced the future as an atheist, and what changed, or did not, in the way he faces it now. The paragraph that begins with his coming to faith from atheism is written to stand without it.
Beside Matthew 6:32 (your heavenly Father knows what you need), James could add what it has meant to trust a Father with the future as a man raised without a father.

The end-times answer states only the creedal center and leaves the timeline open, as a second-order question. If James wants to say where he lands on the millennium and the order of events, it belongs there, in his own words.

reviewed.notes: Second-pass review, done in full from the top; node scripts/validate-needs.mjs fear-of-the-future is clean. Truth: every quotation in the prose was checked with node scripts/bsb.mjs against the verse it cites, and all match. Augustine confirmed through search-engine excerpts of Britannica (direct fetches are blocked here): Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome in 410, pagans blamed Christianity, and The City of God was written about 413 to 426; the two cities are now described as Augustine framed them, the city of God being those who love God (source added: The City of God 14.28). The Psalm 23:4 Hebrew note was checked against the site's STEPBible lexicon (H6757: death-shadow, deep darkness; figuratively distress, extreme danger, the place of the dead), and any extreme danger was narrowed to match. Softened or corrected: Psalm 23 now carries David's name (the site's own note says many scholars read the title as marking a collection); every passage above became several; for most of the West's history became for centuries; the Jeremiah 29:10 paraphrase now follows the text (Babylon's seventy years); Jesus praises the builder (Luke 14:28) became takes it for granted; the Luke 21 answer no longer puts Romans 8 in Jesus' mouth; step 3 no longer calls Psalm 23:4 something God said; the Isaiah 41:10 reading no longer claims the command rests only on God's presence or repeats the answer's closing antithesis. Added James 4:15 to the planning answer and Hebrews 1:2 to the end-times answer, which still leaves the timeline open (slot kept for James's landing; the linked study guide states all three millennial views without crowning one). First person is stance only (five sons; came to faith from atheism). Voice: removed a doubled not-X-Y in Habakkuk and in step 1, the recipe-for cliche, the parent sentence's triplet, and phrasing that duplicated the anxiety page's news paragraph; the atheism paragraph concedes the unbeliever's courage and names what it cannot offer.
